title: Θεοκλυμένου ὄψις
about: Ctesippus, a suitor, throws an ox’s foot at the beggar, who turns his head aside, and the foot strikes the wall. Telemachus rebukes him sharply and says he can no longer bear to watch the house eaten up and the guests ill-used. Agelaus, speaking for calm, repeats a peacemaker’s words, then argues that Odysseus will not return and that Telemachus should urge his mother to marry the best bidder. Telemachus refuses to force her out. Athena then unhinges the suitors’ wits: they laugh with jaws that are not their own and eat bloody meat. The seer Theoclymenus sees night, blood, and phantoms filling the hall, and the suitors laugh at him. He walks out, warning them. They mock Telemachus for his guests and propose selling them to the Sicels. Telemachus says nothing and waits for his father’s signal, while Penelope, at her seat opposite, hears it all, and the narrator says that the suitors are preparing a supper of their own undoing.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἔρριψε βοὸς πόδα χειρὶ παχείῃ.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he threw an ox’s foot with his thick hand.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and threw an ox’s foot with his thick hand.
sentences.n: The thrower is Ctesippus, the suitor whose speech ended at 298; he is named at 303. ὣς εἰπών 'so having spoken' (aorist participle) ties the act to his words. ἔρριψε is the aorist of ῥίπτω 'throw', with the ρ doubled after the augment. βοὸς πόδα is 'an ox’s foot', the lower leg of a slaughtered ox; βοός is the genitive of βοῦς. In παχείῃ the dative ending is Ionic -ῃ, where Attic has -ᾳ: 'with a thick hand'. Murray puts a full stop here, although the next line adds a participle that belongs to the same sentence, and the units follow his punctuation.

sentences.t: κείμενον ἐκ κανέοιο λαβών·
sentences.l: as it lay, out of the basket having taken it;
sentences.i: He had taken it from the basket where it lay;
sentences.n: κείμενον is the present participle of κεῖμαι 'lie' and agrees with πόδα: 'as it lay'. λαβών is the aorist participle of λαμβάνω 'take'; the taking comes before the throw, so the English says 'had taken'. The clause is an afterthought that trails behind the finite verb of 299. κανέοιο is the genitive of κάνεον 'basket' with the Homeric ending -οιο (Attic -ου), governed by ἐκ 'out of'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἀλεύατ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἦκα παρακλίνας κεφαλήν, μείδησε δὲ θυμῷ
σαρδάνιον μάλα τοῖον·
sentences.i: But Odysseus avoided it, bending his head gently aside, and in his heart he smiled a very bitter smile;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ changes the subject: 'he' is Odysseus, as the name at the end of the line shows. The beggar is the target of the throw. ἀλεύατ’ is the elided, unaugmented aorist ἀλεύατο of ἀλεύομαι 'avoid, dodge'. ἦκα is 'gently, slightly', and παρακλίνας is the aorist participle of παρακλίνω 'bend aside': he moves his head just enough. μείδησε is the aorist of μειδάω 'smile', and θυμῷ 'in his heart' makes the smile an inward one. σαρδάνιον is an adverbial accusative of a rare adjective whose meaning is not known; 'bitter, mocking' is the traditional guess (the English 'sardonic' descends from this word). μάλα τοῖον is literally 'very much of that kind', an intensifier whose exact force is also uncertain.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ εὔδμητον βάλε τοῖχον.
sentences.l: And it struck the well-constructed wall.
sentences.i: and it struck the well-constructed wall.
sentences.n: A second ὁ δέ, and a second change of subject: this ὁ is the ox’s foot (πούς is masculine), not Odysseus. βάλε is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω, here 'struck'. εὔδμητον is ἐύδμητος 'well-constructed' (ἐύ- 'well' and the root of δέμω 'build'), agreeing with τοῖχον 'wall'. The throw misses.

sentences.t: Κτήσιππον δ’ ἄρα Τηλέμαχος ἠνίπαπε μύθῳ·
sentences.l: And Ctesippus then Telemachus rebuked with a word:
sentences.i: Then Telemachus rebuked Ctesippus in these words:
sentences.n: Ctesippus is named here for the first time in this part: he is the man who threw. Κτήσιππον is the object, placed first, and Τηλέμαχος the subject. δ’ ἄρα is 'and then'. ἠνίπαπε is the aorist of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke', an aorist with a reduplicated stem (beside ἐνένιπε). μύθῳ is 'with a word' (Attic λόγῳ). The colon introduces the speech, which Murray prints without quotation marks.

sentences.t: Κτήσιππ’, ἦ μάλα τοι τόδε κέρδιον ἔπλετο θυμῷ·
sentences.l: “Ctesippus, truly this has proved much better for you in your heart;
sentences.i: “Ctesippus, this has turned out far better for you, in your heart;
sentences.n: Telemachus’ speech begins. Κτήσιππ’ is the elided vocative Κτήσιππε. ἦ μάλα is 'truly, very much', and τοι is the enclitic dative 'for you' (Attic σοι). κέρδιον is a comparative, 'better, more to one’s profit'. ἔπλετο is the epic past of πέλομαι 'turn out, prove to be'. θυμῷ 'in your heart' is a dative of respect, 'as far as your heart is concerned'. The reason follows in 305–307.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἔβαλες τὸν ξεῖνον· ἀλεύατο γὰρ βέλος αὐτός.
sentences.l: you did not hit the stranger; for he himself avoided the missile.
sentences.i: You did not hit the stranger, for he himself avoided the missile.
sentences.n: ἔβαλες is the aorist of βάλλω, here 'you hit' (the verb also means 'throw at'). τὸν ξεῖνον 'the stranger' is Odysseus. ἀλεύατο repeats the verb of 300, so Telemachus has seen what the narrator reported. γάρ gives the reason, and αὐτός 'himself' stresses that the escape was Odysseus’ own doing. βέλος is any thrown missile, here the ox’s foot.

sentences.t:
ἦ γάρ κέν σε μέσον βάλον ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι,
καί κέ τοι ἀντὶ γάμοιο πατὴρ τάφον ἀμφεπονεῖτο
ἐνθάδε.
sentences.l:
For truly I would have hit you in the middle with a sharp spear,
and for you, instead of a wedding, your father would have been busy about a burial
here.
sentences.i: For I would have struck you through the middle with my sharp spear, and in place of a wedding your father would have been busy here with your burial.
sentences.n: This is the unfulfilled past: κεν with the aorist βάλον 'I would have hit' and κεν with the imperfect ἀμφεπονεῖτο 'would have been busy'. σε μέσον is 'you in the middle', that is, through the body. ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι is a dative, 'with a sharp spear' (ἔγχος 'spear', ὀξυόεις 'sharp, pointed'). τοι is 'for you'. ἀντὶ γάμοιο, 'instead of a wedding', points at Ctesippus’ courtship: his father would be busy with a funeral in place of a marriage. τάφος is 'burial'. ἀμφεπονεῖτο is from ἀμφιπονέομαι 'busy oneself about'. Murray’s full stop falls after ἐνθάδε 'here', in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
τῷ μή τίς μοι ἀεικείας ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
φαινέτω·
sentences.l:
Therefore let no one to me unseemliness in the house
show;
sentences.i: So let no one show me unseemly behaviour in my house;
sentences.n: τῷ is the article-form used as an adverb, 'therefore' (literally 'by that'). μή τις … φαινέτω is a prohibition with the third-person imperative of φαίνω 'show': 'let no one show'. ἀεικείας is the accusative plural of ἀείκεια 'unseemly treatment, unseemliness', from the same root as ἀεικέα and ἀεικελίως, which return in 317 and 319. μοι is 'before me, to me'. ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is ἐν οἴκῳ 'in the house', with the longer form ἐνί. This unit starts in the middle of 308 and ends with the first word of 309.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γὰρ νοέω καὶ οἶδα ἕκαστα,
ἐσθλά τε καὶ τὰ χέρηα· πάρος δ’ ἔτι νήπιος ἦα.
sentences.l:
for now I perceive and know each thing,
both good things and the worse; but before, still a child I was.
sentences.i: for now I understand and know everything, the good and the worse alike; before this I was still a child.
sentences.n: νοέω is 'I perceive, understand' and οἶδα 'I know'; ἕκαστα is neuter plural, 'each thing'. ἐσθλά 'good things' is answered by τὰ χέρηα 'the worse ones', where χέρηα is the neuter plural of the epic adjective χέρης (Attic χείρων, neuter plural χείρω). πάρος is 'before', and ἦα is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). νήπιος usually means 'foolish', as in the proem; with πάρος and ἔτι 'still' it means 'a child'. Telemachus is claiming that he has grown up.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔμπης τάδε μὲν καὶ τέτλαμεν εἰσορόωντες,
μήλων σφαζομένων οἴνοιό τε πινομένοιο
καὶ σίτου·
sentences.i: But all the same, we endure these things, looking on as flocks are slaughtered and wine is drunk and food consumed;
sentences.n: ἔμπης is 'all the same, nevertheless'. τέτλαμεν is the perfect of τλάω 'endure', with present meaning, and εἰσορόωντες is the uncontracted participle (Attic εἰσορῶντες) 'looking on'. The three genitives are a genitive absolute: μήλων 'flocks' (sheep and goats together), οἴνοιο with the ending -οιο, and σίτου 'food'. The first two have participles, σφαζομένων 'being slaughtered' and πινομένοιο 'being drunk'; with σίτου none is written, and the English supplies 'consumed'. The ano teleia after σίτου ends the unit.

sentences.t: χαλεπὸν γὰρ ἐρυκακέειν ἕνα πολλούς.
sentences.l: for it is hard for one to hold back many.
sentences.i: for it is hard for one man to hold back many.
sentences.n: Telemachus gives the reason for his patience. ἐρυκακέειν is a reduplicated aorist infinitive of ἐρύκω 'hold back, restrain' (Attic ἐρύκειν). ἕνα πολλούς, 'one … many', puts the two numbers side by side: ἕνα is the accusative subject of the infinitive and πολλούς its object, as in the general statement 'one man restrains many only with difficulty'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μηκέτι μοι κακὰ ῥέζετε δυσμενέοντες·
sentences.l: But come, no longer to me evil things do, being hostile;
sentences.i: But come now, no longer do evil to me in your hostility;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come now'. μηκέτι 'no longer' with the present imperative ῥέζετε (ῥέζω 'do') means 'stop doing'. κακά is 'evil things', object of the verb, and μοι is 'to me'. δυσμενέοντες is the uncontracted participle (Attic δυσμενοῦντες) 'being ill-disposed, hostile'; the English makes it a phrase, 'in your hostility'.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἤδη μ’ αὐτὸν κτεῖναι μενεαίνετε χαλκῷ,
sentences.l: But if now me myself to kill you are eager with bronze,
sentences.i: But if you are already set on killing me myself with bronze,
sentences.n: εἰ δέ 'but if'; μ’ αὐτόν 'me myself'; κτεῖναι is the aorist infinitive of κτείνω 'kill', after μενεαίνετε 'you are eager, set on'. χαλκῷ is 'with bronze', that is, with a weapon. The clause is the condition only; the main clause comes in the next two lines.

sentences.t:
καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην, καί κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη
τεθνάμεν ἢ τάδε γ’ αἰὲν ἀεικέα ἔργ’ ὁράασθαι,
ξείνους τε στυφελιζομένους δμῳάς τε γυναῖκας
ῥυστάζοντας ἀεικελίως κατὰ δώματα καλά.
sentences.l:
even that I should wish, and much better it would be
to be dead than these always unseemly deeds to look upon,
strangers roughly handled, and the maidservant women
(the men) dragging about in unseemly ways through the fine house.”
sentences.i: I should wish even that, and it would be far better to be dead than to keep seeing these unseemly deeds, strangers roughly handled, and the suitors dragging the maidservants about in unseemly ways through the fine house.”
sentences.n: καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην 'I would wish even that' and κέρδιον εἴη 'it would be better' are the main clause to the condition of 315, both optatives with κε. τεθνάμεν is the perfect infinitive of θνήσκω 'to be dead' (Attic τεθνάναι). The accusatives of 318–319 continue ὁράασθαι 'to look upon' from 317: στυφελιζομένους 'roughly handled' is a passive participle, and ῥυστάζοντας is masculine, so the dragging is done by men who are not named, and the maidservants, δμῳάς … γυναῖκας, are dragged. ἀεικελίως is the adverb 'in unseemly ways'; δώματα καλά is plural in form but means the one fine house. Telemachus borrows familiar words: 316 is also said by Odysseus at 11.358, 317 is Telemachus’ own at 16.107, and 318–319 are 16.108–109. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ 'so he spoke' is ἔφατο, elided (the τ becomes θ before the rough breathing of οἱ), a middle form of φημί. The reaction formula returns word for word from 8.234. ἀκήν is a fixed accusative used as an adverb, 'silent, still', and σιωπῇ is the dative 'in silence'; the English gives each word its own adjective.

sentences.t: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε Δαμαστορίδης Ἀγέλαος·
sentences.l: But late indeed spoke among them Damastor’s son, Agelaus:
sentences.i: At last Agelaus, son of Damastor, spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὀψέ 'late' with δὲ δή marks that only now, after the silence, someone finds a voice: 'at last'. μετέειπε is the aorist of μετεῖπον 'speak among', used when a speaker addresses a gathering. Δαμαστορίδης is a patronymic, 'son of Damastor', made with the suffix -ίδης. Agelaus is one of the suitors, and the line is the speech-introduction.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐκ ἂν δή τις ἐπὶ ῥηθέντι δικαίῳ
ἀντιβίοις ἐπέεσσι καθαπτόμενος χαλεπαίνοι·
sentences.l:
“O friends, not would indeed anyone, at a just thing said,
with hostile words accosting, be angry;
sentences.i: “Friends, surely no one should take offence at a just remark and address the speaker directly with hostile words;
sentences.n: Agelaus speaks as the peacemaker, and he borrows the words of Amphinomus at 18.414–415. οὐκ ἂν δή τις … χαλεπαίνοι is the optative with ἄν used as a mild prohibition: 'no one would be angry', that is, 'no one should be'. ἐπὶ ῥηθέντι δικαίῳ is 'at a just thing said' (ῥηθέντι is the aorist passive participle of λέγω). ἀντιβίοις ἐπέεσσι is a dative of means with ἐπέεσσι in the Homeric -εσσι ending: 'with hostile words'. καθαπτόμενος is 'accosting, addressing'.

sentences.t:
μήτε τι τὸν ξεῖνον στυφελίζετε μήτε τιν’ ἄλλον
δμώων, οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
sentences.l:
Neither in any way the stranger handle roughly, nor any other
of the servants who are throughout the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.i: Do not handle the stranger roughly, nor any other of the servants in the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.n: Agelaus now turns the same plea, from 18.416–417, to the stranger and the household. μήτε … μήτε with the present imperative στυφελίζετε means 'do not go on handling roughly'. τὸν ξεῖνον is the stranger, Odysseus. ἄλλον δμώων is a partitive genitive, 'any other of the servants', and in the relative clause οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο the verb 'are' is left to be understood. δώματ’ is plural for a single house. Ὀδυσσῆος has double σ here, where line 329 has Ὀδυσῆα with one.

sentences.t:
Τηλεμάχῳ δέ κε μῦθον ἐγὼ καὶ μητέρι φαίην
ἤπιον, εἴ σφωϊν κραδίῃ ἅδοι ἀμφοτέροιϊν.
sentences.l:
But to Telemachus a word I would say, and to his mother,
a gentle one, if to you two in heart it would be pleasing, to both.
sentences.i: I would speak a gentle word to Telemachus and to his mother, if it were pleasing to the heart of you both.
sentences.n: φαίην is the optative of φημί, 'I would say', with κε. Telemachus and his mother are named in the third person, as dative objects (Τηλεμάχῳ … μητέρι). μῦθον ἤπιον is 'a gentle word'. εἰ … ἅδοι is the optative of ἁνδάνω 'be pleasing', in a condition that is only imagined. σφωϊν and ἀμφοτέροιϊν are dual forms, 'to you two' and 'to both': the speech slips from talking about the pair to talking to them. κραδίῃ is the dative 'in the heart'.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν ὑμῖν θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐώλπει
νοστήσειν Ὀδυσῆα πολύφρονα ὅνδε δόμονδε,
sentences.l:
As long as to you the heart in your breasts was hoping
that Odysseus, much-minded, would come home to this house,
sentences.i: For as long as the heart in your breasts hoped that Odysseus of the many counsels would come home to this house,
sentences.n: ὄφρα μέν … τόφρα (330) is the pair 'as long as … for so long'. ὑμῖν, 'to you', is a dative of possession: the heart is theirs. θυμός stands for the feeling heart, ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν 'in the breasts'. ἐώλπει is the past of ἔλπομαι 'hope', and νοστήσειν is the future infinitive of νοστέω 'return home' (cf. νόστος). Ὀδυσῆα is the accusative with the Ionic single σ. πολύφρονα is 'much-minded', one of Odysseus’ epithets. ὅνδε is the accusative of ὅδε 'this' and goes with δόμονδε 'to the house' (the suffix -δε gives direction): 'to this house', the one in which they stand.

sentences.t:
τόφρ’ οὔ τις νέμεσις μενέμεν τ’ ἦν ἰσχέμεναί τε
μνηστῆρας κατὰ δώματ’, ἐπεὶ τόδε κέρδιον ἦεν,
εἰ νόστησ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ ὑπότροπος ἵκετο δῶμα·
sentences.i: for so long it was no cause for resentment that the suitors stayed on and held back in the house, since that was the better course, if Odysseus came home and arrived back at his house;
sentences.n: τόφρα answers ὄφρα in 328. νέμεσις is righteous resentment, the feeling that a wrong has been done and ought to be blamed. The two infinitives μενέμεν (= μένειν) and ἰσχέμεναι (= ἴσχειν) have μνηστῆρας as their accusative subject: 'no resentment that the suitors stay and hold back'. What the suitors 'hold back' from is not said; 'hold off, wait' is the sense wanted. ἦεν is ἦν. In the last line εἰ with the aorists νόστησ’ (elided νόστησε) and ἵκετο (unaugmented) imagines Odysseus’ return as something that might have happened; ὑπότροπος means 'turning back, returning'. The ano teleia ends the unit; the sentence from 328 to 332 would otherwise fill five lines, so it is cut at the comma after 329.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἤδη τόδε δῆλον, ὅ τ’ οὐκέτι νόστιμός ἐστιν.
sentences.l: But now already this is clear, that no longer is he one to return.
sentences.i: But now it is already clear that he is no longer going to come home.
sentences.n: ὅ τε, written ὅ τ’ before the vowel, is the neuter relative used as a conjunction, 'that', as ὅτι is in Attic. νόστιμος is 'having a homecoming, destined to return'; with οὐκέτι it means 'no longer to return'. δῆλον is 'plain, clear'. Agelaus presents Odysseus’ death as a conclusion that everyone can now draw; it is argument, not information.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε, σῇ τάδε μητρὶ παρεζόμενος κατάλεξον,
γήμασθ’ ὅς τις ἄριστος ἀνὴρ καὶ πλεῖστα πόρῃσιν,
ὄφρα σὺ μὲν χαίρων πατρώϊα πάντα νέμηαι,
ἔσθων καὶ πίνων, ἡ δ’ ἄλλου δῶμα κομίζῃ.
sentences.l:
But come, to your mother these things, sitting beside her, tell,
to marry whichever man is best and may give the most,
so that you, rejoicing, all your paternal possessions may enjoy,
eating and drinking, and she another’s house may tend.”
sentences.i: But come now, sit beside your mother and tell her this: to marry whichever man is best and gives the most, so that you may enjoy all your father’s property and be glad, eating and drinking, while she looks after another man’s house.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come now', and κατάλεξον, the aorist imperative of καταλέγω, is here 'tell' with the infinitive: 'tell her to marry'. σῇ is the possessive 'your', παρεζόμενος 'sitting beside'. γήμασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive, said of a woman, 'to marry, take a husband'. ὅς τις ἄριστος ἀνὴρ καὶ πλεῖστα πόρῃσιν, with πόρῃσιν the aorist subjunctive of πορεῖν 'give', means the man who offers the most, the bridal gifts being understood. νέμηαι is the middle subjunctive (= νέμῃ) 'enjoy the use of'; πατρώϊα are 'one’s father’s possessions'. ἔσθων is ἐσθίων. ἡ δ’ is 'and she', and κομίζῃ 'tend, look after'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: Telemachus answers Agelaus with his own standing reply-formula. ἀντίον ηὔδα is 'spoke face to face' (ηὔδα is the augmented imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'); αὖ is 'in turn', and πεπνυμένος is his regular epithet, 'prudent'. The line recurs word for word from 1.388.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰ Ζῆν’, Ἀγέλαε, καὶ ἄλγεα πατρὸς ἐμοῖο,
ὅς που τῆλ’ Ἰθάκης ἢ ἔφθιται ἢ ἀλάληται,
οὔ τι διατρίβω μητρὸς γάμον, ἀλλὰ κελεύω
γήμασθ’ ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃ, ποτὶ δ’ ἄσπετα δῶρα δίδωμι.
sentences.l:
“No, by Zeus, Agelaus, and by the pains of my father,
who somewhere far from Ithaca either has perished or is wandering,
I do not at all delay my mother’s marriage, but I urge her
to marry whom she wishes, and besides boundless gifts I give.
sentences.i: “No, by Zeus, Agelaus, and by the pains of my father, who is somewhere far from Ithaca, either dead or wandering, I am not holding up my mother’s marriage; I urge her to marry whomever she wishes, and I add boundless gifts besides.
sentences.n: οὐ μά is the negative oath formula 'no, by …', with the accusative Ζῆν’ (Ζῆνα, elided) of the god sworn by; καὶ ἄλγεα πατρὸς ἐμοῖο adds a second thing sworn by, 'and by my father’s pains' (ἐμοῖο = ἐμοῦ). The relative clause says that the father is 'somewhere far from Ithaca', and ἔφθιται (perfect of φθίνω 'perish') and ἀλάληται (perfect of ἀλάομαι 'wander') give the two possibilities. διατρίβω is 'rub away', hence 'delay'. κελεύω γήμασθαι is 'I bid her marry'; ᾧ κ’ ἐθέλῃ is 'to whom she may wish'. ποτί is πρός used as an adverb, 'in addition', and ἄσπετα 'boundless'.

sentences.t:
αἰδέομαι δ’ ἀέκουσαν ἀπὸ μεγάροιο δίεσθαι
μύθῳ ἀναγκαίῳ· μὴ τοῦτο θεὸς τελέσειεν.
sentences.l:
I am ashamed to drive her, unwilling, from the hall
with a word of compulsion; may a god not bring this to pass.”
sentences.i: But I am ashamed to drive her from the hall against her will with a compelling word; may no god bring that about.”
sentences.n: αἰδέομαι is 'I feel shame at, I shrink from', with an infinitive. ἀέκουσαν is the feminine accusative 'unwilling' (Attic ἄκουσαν), and δίεσθαι the infinitive of δίεμαι 'drive off'. μύθῳ ἀναγκαίῳ is 'with a word of compulsion', that is, an order she could not refuse. μὴ τοῦτο θεὸς τελέσειεν is a wish with μή and the optative of τελέω 'bring to pass'. Telemachus will not himself send his mother out of the house. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο Τηλέμαχος·
sentences.l: So spoke Telemachus;
sentences.i: So spoke Telemachus;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is 'so he spoke', φάτο being the unaugmented aorist of φημί, here with the speaker’s name in place of 'he'. The formula closes a speech and begins a paragraph of narration, with Telemachus’ words complete.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρσι δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
ἄσβεστον γέλω ὦρσε, παρέπλαγξεν δὲ νόημα.
sentences.l:
and among the suitors Pallas Athena
unquenchable laughter roused, and made their thought stray aside.
sentences.i: But Pallas Athena roused laughter that would never go out among the suitors, and led their thoughts astray.
sentences.n: μνηστῆρσι is the dative 'among the suitors, in them'. ἄσβεστος is 'unquenchable', built on σβέννυμι 'quench', so the laughter is pictured as a fire that will not go out. γέλω is the accusative of γέλως 'laughter'. ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι 'rouse, stir up'. παρέπλαγξεν is the aorist of παραπλάζω 'make stray, lead astray', and νόημα is 'thought, mind'; the singular stands for the minds of all of them. Athena’s hand is shown at work, as the narrator reports it.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἤδη γναθμοῖσι γελοίων ἀλλοτρίοισιν,
αἱμοφόρυκτα δὲ δὴ κρέα ἤσθιον·
sentences.l:
And they now with others’ jaws were laughing,
and blood-smeared indeed the meat they ate;
sentences.i: and now they laughed with jaws that were not their own, and ate meat smeared with blood;
sentences.n: γελοίων is an imperfect of γελοιάω, a by-form of γελάω, 'were laughing', and ἤσθιον the imperfect of ἐσθίω 'eat'. γναθμοῖσι … ἀλλοτρίοισιν is a dative of means, 'with jaws belonging to others', which means that the laughter is not theirs. αἱμοφόρυκτα is a rare compound of αἷμα 'blood' and the root of φύρω 'mix, smear', 'smeared with blood'; whether the meat is raw or only bloody is not said. δὴ adds emphasis. The ano teleia after ἤσθιον ends the unit in the middle of 348.

sentences.t:
ὄσσε δ’ ἄρα σφέων
δακρυόφιν πίμπλαντο, γόον δ’ ὠΐετο θυμός.
sentences.l:
and their eyes then of them
with tears were filled, and lament their heart foreboded.
sentences.i: their eyes filled with tears, and their hearts foreboded lament.
sentences.n: ὄσσε is a dual, 'the two eyes', used with a plural verb, πίμπλαντο, the imperfect passive of πίμπλημι 'fill'. σφέων is the epic genitive 'of them' (Attic σφῶν). δακρυόφιν has the suffix -φι(ν), which here gives the instrument: 'with tears'. γόον is 'lament, wailing'. ὠΐετο is the imperfect of ὀΐομαι 'suppose, expect, forebode', and θυμός is 'heart'; the heart sees the lament that is coming.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Theoclymenus, godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: And Theoclymenus, godlike in form, spoke up among them as well:
sentences.n: The speech-introduction names the next speaker, Theoclymenus, who the suitors’ words at 380 show to be a prophet. τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε is 'and among them spoke also'; τοῖσι is the Homeric dative plural of the article-form, 'them'. θεοειδής 'godlike in form' is his regular epithet, built on θεός and εἶδος 'form'. The line is repeated from 17.151.

sentences.t: ἆ δειλοί, τί κακὸν τόδε πάσχετε;
sentences.l: “Oh, miserable ones, what evil is this you suffer?
sentences.i: “Oh, you miserable men, what is this evil that you are suffering?
sentences.n: ἆ is an exclamation. δειλοί, vocative plural of δειλός, is 'miserable, wretched' (the Homeric word is pity, not an accusation of cowardice). τί κακὸν τόδε πάσχετε is 'what evil is this you suffer?', with the neuter τί 'what' and κακὸν τόδε 'this evil'. The Greek question mark is the sign ; and looks like a semicolon. What Theoclymenus describes is a vision of the future; the suitors, who laugh at him in 358, do not see it.

sentences.t:
νυκτὶ μὲν ὑμέων
εἰλύαται κεφαλαί τε πρόσωπά τε νέρθε τε γοῦνα.
sentences.l:
In night, of you,
are wrapped both the heads and the faces and below the knees.
sentences.i: Your heads and faces and, below, your knees are wrapped in night.
sentences.n: εἰλύαται is the perfect passive, third plural, of εἰλύω 'wrap, enfold'; νυκτί is a dative, 'in night'. The list runs from the top downward: κεφαλαί 'heads', πρόσωπα 'faces', and νέρθε τε γοῦνα 'and below, the knees'; γοῦνα is the short form of γόνατα. ὑμέων is the epic genitive of σύ in the plural, 'of you' (Attic ὑμῶν). The three τε … τε … τε give the sense of a thing seen part by part, in order.

sentences.t:
οἰμωγὴ δὲ δέδηε, δεδάκρυνται δὲ παρειαί,
αἵματι δ’ ἐρράδαται τοῖχοι καλαί τε μεσόδμαι·
sentences.l:
and wailing is ablaze, and wet with tears are your cheeks,
and with blood are sprinkled the walls and the fine cross-timbers;
sentences.i: Wailing is ablaze, your cheeks are wet with tears, and the walls and the fine cross-timbers are sprinkled with blood;
sentences.n: οἰμωγή is 'wailing'. δέδηε is the perfect of δαίω 'burn' used intransitively, 'is ablaze'. δεδάκρυνται is a perfect passive of δακρύω 'weep', 'have been wet with tears', and ἐρράδαται a perfect passive of ῥαίνω 'sprinkle'. All the perfects describe a condition that already exists. τοῖχοι are 'walls'. μεσόδμαι are cross-timbers or beams of the hall, and their exact fitting is not known. αἵματι is the dative 'with blood'.

sentences.t:
εἰδώλων δὲ πλέον πρόθυρον, πλείη δὲ καὶ αὐλή,
ἱεμένων Ἔρεβόσδε ὑπὸ ζόφον·
sentences.l:
and of phantoms full is the forecourt, and full too the courtyard,
of them hastening to Erebus beneath the gloom;
sentences.i: The forecourt is full of phantoms, and the courtyard too, phantoms hastening down to Erebus, beneath the gloom;
sentences.n: εἰδώλων is the genitive plural of εἴδωλον 'phantom'. πλέον and πλείη are the neuter and feminine of 'full', and each takes a genitive: 'full of phantoms'. πρόθυρον is the forecourt before the doors, and αὐλή the open courtyard. ἱεμένων is the present middle participle of ἵημι 'hasten, rush', genitive plural and agreeing with εἰδώλων. Ἔρεβόσδε has the suffix -δε 'to': 'to Erebus', the dark place under the earth. ὑπὸ ζόφον, with the accusative, is 'down under the gloom'. The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of 356.

sentences.t:
ἠέλιος δὲ
οὐρανοῦ ἐξαπόλωλε, κακὴ δ’ ἐπιδέδρομεν ἀχλύς.
sentences.l:
and the sun
from the sky has perished, and an evil haze has run over.”
sentences.i: and the sun has vanished from the sky, and an evil haze has come sweeping over.”
sentences.n: ἠέλιος is the sun, and ἐξαπόλωλε is the perfect of ἐξαπόλλυμι, 'has perished utterly', here 'has vanished'. οὐρανοῦ is the genitive 'from the sky'. ἐπιδέδρομεν is the perfect of ἐπιτρέχω 'run over, spread across'; the verb has no object in the Greek, and the haze spreads over everything he sees. κακὴ ἀχλύς is 'an evil haze'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἡδὺ γέλασσαν.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all at him sweetly laughed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all laughed pleasantly at him.
sentences.n: The suitors laugh at the vision. ἡδύ is the neuter adjective used as an adverb, 'sweetly, pleasantly', so the laughter is untroubled, not forced. ἐπ’ αὐτῷ is 'at him' (ἐπί with the dative). γέλασσαν is the unaugmented aorist of γελάω (Attic ἐγέλασαν). This is the second laugh of the scene, after the unnatural laughter of 347.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς, ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν·
sentences.l: And among them Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, began to speak-in-assembly:
sentences.i: Eurymachus, son of Polybus, was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: Eurymachus answers for the suitors. ἦρχ’ is ἦρχε, the imperfect of ἄρχω 'begin, lead', and ἀγορεύειν is 'to speak' (in an assembly or among a company). With the infinitive, ἦρχε ἀγορεύειν is 'was the first to speak'. Πολύβου πάϊς is 'son of Polybus', πάϊς being the epic form of παῖς. The line is repeated from 16.345.

sentences.t: ἀφραίνει ξεῖνος νέον ἄλλοθεν εἰληλουθώς.
sentences.l: “Senseless is the stranger, newly come from elsewhere.
sentences.i: “The stranger is out of his senses; he has only just come from somewhere else.
sentences.n: ἀφραίνει is 'is senseless', a verb formed from ἄφρων 'without sense'. νέον is the adverb 'newly, just now', and ἄλλοθεν 'from elsewhere' has the suffix -θεν 'from'. εἰληλουθώς is the perfect participle of ἔρχομαι, 'having come'. Eurymachus treats the vision as the raving of a newcomer who does not know the place.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μιν αἶψα, νέοι, δόμου ἐκπέμψασθε θύραζε
εἰς ἀγορὴν ἔρχεσθαι, ἐπεὶ τάδε νυκτὶ ἐΐσκει.
sentences.l:
But him quickly, young men, out of the house send away, outdoors,
to go to the assembly, since these things to night he likens.”
sentences.i: Come then, young men, quickly send him out of the house, out of doors, to go to the assembly, since he takes all this for night.”
sentences.n: μιν is the enclitic 'him'. νέοι is the vocative 'young men', here the other suitors. δόμου is a genitive of separation, 'from the house'; ἐκπέμψασθε is the aorist middle imperative of ἐκπέμπω 'send out'; θύραζε is 'out of doors' (the suffix -ζε is -δε). εἰς ἀγορὴν ἔρχεσθαι is an infinitive of purpose: 'so that he may go to the assembly', out in the open. ἐΐσκει is from ἐΐσκω 'liken, take to be': he takes these surroundings for night. The implied joke is that outside, in the open, he will find it is day. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Theoclymenus, godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Then Theoclymenus, godlike in form, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula. προσέειπε is 'addressed', τὸν δ’ αὖτε 'and him in turn', and Θεοκλύμενος θεοειδής the speaker with his regular epithet. The line is repeated from 15.271.

sentences.t: Εὐρύμαχ’, οὔ τί σ’ ἄνωγα ἐμοὶ πομπῆας ὀπάζειν·
sentences.l: “Eurymachus, not at all do I bid you to assign me escorts;
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, I do not ask you to assign me escorts;
sentences.n: Εὐρύμαχ’ is the elided vocative. ἄνωγα is a perfect with present sense, 'I bid, I ask'. οὔ τί σ’ is 'not at all you'. πομπῆας is the accusative plural of πομπεύς 'escort, conductor', and ὀπάζειν the infinitive of ὀπάζω 'assign as attendant'. Theoclymenus turns down the offer of an escort out of the house.

sentences.t:
εἰσί μοι ὀφθαλμοί τε καὶ οὔατα καὶ πόδες ἄμφω
καὶ νόος ἐν στήθεσσι τετυγμένος οὐδὲν ἀεικής.
sentences.l:
There are for me eyes and ears and feet, both,
and a mind in my breast, wrought in no way unseemly.
sentences.i: I have eyes and ears and both my feet, and a mind in my breast that is well wrought, with nothing unseemly in it.
sentences.n: εἰσί μοι is 'there are to me', a dative of possession for 'I have'. οὔατα is the plural of οὖς 'ear', and πόδες ἄμφω 'both feet'. νόος is the uncontracted form of νοῦς 'mind'. τετυγμένος is the perfect passive participle of τεύχω 'fashion', as of a well-made object, and οὐδὲν ἀεικής, 'in no way unseemly', is an understatement: his mind is sound. He answers the idea that he needs a guide by listing the faculties that would guide him.

sentences.t:
τοῖς ἔξειμι θύραζε, ἐπεὶ νοέω κακὸν ὔμμιν
ἐρχόμενον, τό κεν οὔ τις ὑπεκφύγοι οὐδ’ ἀλέαιτο
μνηστήρων, οἳ δῶμα κάτ’ ἀντιθέου Ὀδυσῆος
ἀνέρας ὑβρίζοντες ἀτάσθαλα μηχανάασθε.
sentences.l:
With these I shall go out of doors, since I perceive an evil for you
coming, which not one would escape or avoid
of the suitors, who throughout the house of godlike Odysseus
insulting men wanton things devise.”
sentences.i: With these I shall go out of doors, since I see an evil coming upon you, which not one of you suitors could escape or avoid, you who in the house of godlike Odysseus outrage men and devise wanton deeds.”
sentences.n: τοῖς, 'with these', points back to the eyes, ears, feet and mind of 365–366. ἔξειμι (ἐκ + εἶμι) is a present form with future sense, 'I shall go out'. νοέω is 'I perceive', and ὔμμιν is the epic form of ὑμῖν. τό κεν οὔ τις ὑπεκφύγοι οὐδ’ ἀλέαιτο is a potential relative clause, 'which none could escape or avoid', and μνηστήρων is a partitive genitive 'of the suitors'. The relative οἳ takes a second-person verb, μηχανάασθε (uncontracted, Attic μηχανᾶσθε), because Theoclymenus turns to speak to them: 'you who'. ὑβρίζοντες is 'acting with violence, outrage', ἀνέρας is ἄνδρας 'men', and ἀτάσθαλα 'wanton deeds'. Ὀδυσῆος has one σ. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐξῆλθε δόμων εὖ ναιεταόντων,
ἵκετο δ’ ἐς Πείραιον, ὅ μιν πρόφρων ὑπέδεκτο.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he went out of the well-inhabited house,
and came to Peiraeus, who him, ready-minded, received.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went out of the well-inhabited house, and came to Peiraeus, who received him with a ready mind.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken', the closing formula for a speaker who then acts. δόμων εὖ ναιεταόντων is 'out of the well-inhabited house', with an uncontracted participle of ναιετάω 'dwell, be inhabited'. ἵκετο is the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι 'come to'. Πείραιον is a man, Peiraeus, and not the port: ὅ μιν πρόφρων ὑπέδεκτο shows him receiving a guest as host, so ἐς Πείραιον means to his house. ὅ is the relative 'who', μιν 'him', and πρόφρων 'ready-minded, willing'. ὑπέδεκτο is the aorist middle of ὑποδέχομαι 'receive as a host'.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐς ἀλλήλους ὁρόωντες
Τηλέμαχον ἐρέθιζον, ἐπὶ ξείνοις γελόωντες·
sentences.l:
And the suitors then all, at one another looking,
provoked Telemachus, laughing at the strangers;
sentences.i: And all the suitors, looking at one another, goaded Telemachus, laughing at his strangers;
sentences.n: ὁρόωντες and γελόωντες are uncontracted participles (Attic ὁρῶντες, γελῶντες). ἐς ἀλλήλους is 'at one another', the glances passing round the table. ἐρέθιζον is the imperfect of ἐρεθίζω 'provoke, goad'. ἐπὶ ξείνοις is 'at the strangers' (ἐπί with the dative, 'over, at'); the plural covers the two guests, Odysseus and Theoclymenus. Line 390 spells the same participle γελοίωντες, the same word in another form.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.l: Thus would someone say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: and one of the overbearing young men would say something like this:
sentences.n: ὧδε is 'thus, in this way', and εἴπεσκε is an iterative past, 'would say', with the suffix -σκ- of repeated action: this is the kind of thing they said. τις is 'someone', so the speaker is one suitor among several. νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων is a partitive genitive, 'of the overbearing young men'. The line is repeated from 2.324.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχ’, οὔ τις σεῖο κακοξεινώτερος ἄλλος·
sentences.l: “Telemachus, no other is worse-in-strangers than you;
sentences.i: “Telemachus, no one else is worse than you where strangers are concerned;
sentences.n: σεῖο is the genitive of comparison, 'than you' (Attic σοῦ). κακοξεινώτερος is the comparative of κακόξεινος (κακός 'bad' and ξεῖνος 'stranger'), and its sense is disputed: either 'worse at treating guests' or, as the next lines suggest, 'worse off in the guests he gets'. The English leaves it open. A suitor mocks Telemachus for the guests he has taken in.

sentences.t:
οἷον μέν τινα τοῦτον ἔχεις ἐπίμαστον ἀλήτην,
σίτου καὶ οἴνου κεχρημένον, οὐδέ τι ἔργων
ἔμπαιον οὐδὲ βίης, ἀλλ’ αὔτως ἄχθος ἀρούρης.
sentences.l:
What a one, this sought-out vagrant that you keep,
in need of food and wine, and not at all of works
skilled, nor of strength, but merely a burden of the plough-land.
sentences.i: What a man you keep in this sought-out vagrant, in need of food and wine, skilled in no work and no strength, merely a burden on the plough-land.
sentences.n: οἷον is exclamatory, 'what a …!'. ἐπίμαστον is a rare adjective that seems to come from ἐπιμαίομαι 'reach for, seek'; 'sought-out' is only a literal guess, and its exact meaning is not known. ἀλήτης is 'vagrant, wanderer'. κεχρημένον is the perfect participle of χράομαι, 'in need of', with the genitives σίτου καὶ οἴνου. ἔμπαιον οὐδὲ βίης is 'skilled in neither work nor strength', with ἔργων 'works' and βίης 'strength' as genitives. ἀλλ’ αὔτως is 'but merely', and ἄχθος ἀρούρης 'a burden of the plough-land', a burden to the very soil.

sentences.t: ἄλλος δ’ αὖτέ τις οὗτος ἀνέστη μαντεύεσθαι.
sentences.l: And another again, this one, has stood up to prophesy.
sentences.i: And now this other one has stood up to prophesy.
sentences.n: ἄλλος … αὖτέ τις οὗτος is 'another, again, this one': the second of the two strangers, Theoclymenus. ἀνέστη is the aorist of ἀνίστημι 'stand up'. μαντεύεσθαι is the infinitive of μαντεύομαι 'prophesy, act as a seer', and it states the purpose.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ εἴ μοί τι πίθοιο, τό κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη·
sentences.l: But if you would obey me at all, that would be much better:
sentences.i: But if you would take my advice at all, that would be far better:
sentences.n: εἴ μοί τι πίθοιο is 'if you would obey me at all' (πείθομαι with the dative, in the optative; τι is adverbial). τό is 'that', and κεν … εἴη gives the result, 'it would be'. πολὺ κέρδιον is 'much better', as in 316. The colon introduces the plan.

sentences.t:
τοὺς ξείνους ἐν νηῒ πολυκληῗδι βαλόντες
ἐς Σικελοὺς πέμψωμεν, ὅθεν κέ τοι ἄξιον ἄλφοι.
sentences.l:
the strangers in a many-thwarted ship having thrown,
to the Sicels let us send, whence for you a worthy price it may fetch.”
sentences.i: Let us put the strangers aboard a ship of many thwarts and send them to the Sicels, from where you would get a worthy price.”
sentences.n: βαλόντες, 'having thrown', is the aorist participle of βάλλω, here meaning 'put aboard'. πολυκληῗδι is 'with many thwarts', κληΐς being the rowing-bench or thwart. Σικελούς is 'the Sicels', a distant people. πέμψωμεν is the aorist subjunctive in a first-person exhortation, 'let us send'. ὅθεν κέ τοι ἄξιον ἄλφοι is 'whence it would fetch you a worthy price': ἄλφοι is the optative of ἀλφάνω 'bring in, fetch', with no subject written; it means that the strangers would be sold. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφασαν μνηστῆρες·
sentences.l: So spoke the suitors;
sentences.i: So spoke the suitors;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφασαν is the plural of the closing formula, 'so they spoke', with the subject μνηστῆρες named; ἔφασαν is the third-person plural of φημί. Telemachus’ silence in the next clause is set against this.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ οὐκ ἐμπάζετο μύθων,
ἀλλ’ ἀκέων πατέρα προσεδέρκετο, δέγμενος αἰεί,
ὁππότε δὴ μνηστῆρσιν ἀναιδέσι χεῖρας ἐφήσει.
sentences.l:
And he took no heed of the words,
but in silence looked toward his father, waiting always
for when upon the shameless suitors he would lay his hands.
sentences.i: But he paid no heed to their words, and looked in silence at his father, always waiting for the moment when he would lay hands on the shameless suitors.
sentences.n: ὁ δέ is 'but he', and he is Telemachus; the suitor’s speech was the last, so the pronoun switches back. ἐμπάζομαι takes the genitive: οὐκ ἐμπάζετο μύθων 'took no heed of the words'. ἀκέων is 'in silence'. πατέρα is 'his father': the narrator calls the beggar so. προσεδέρκετο is 'looked at, looked toward'. δέγμενος is the epic participle of δέχομαι 'await' (= δεχόμενος), with αἰεί 'always'. ὁππότε … ἐφήσει is 'for the time when he will lay on', the future of ἐφίημι; χεῖρας ἐφήσει is 'will set his hands on'. ἀναιδέσι is 'shameless'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ κατ’ ἄντηστιν θεμένη περικαλλέα δίφρον
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
ἀνδρῶν ἐν μεγάροισιν ἑκάστου μῦθον ἄκουεν.
sentences.l:
And she, right opposite having set a very fair stool,
the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope,
of the men in the halls the speech of each was hearing.
sentences.i: And she, the daughter of Icarius, circumspect Penelope, had set a very fair stool right opposite and was listening to the talk of each man in the halls.
sentences.n: ἡ δέ, 'but she', is named in 388 as Penelope, who is introduced as a listener. κατ’ ἄντηστιν is 'directly opposite'; the Greek does not say what she faces, only that she has placed her seat where she can hear. θεμένη is the aorist middle participle of τίθημι, 'having set (for herself)'. δίφρος is 'stool', and περικαλλής 'very fair'. κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο is 'the daughter of Icarius', with the genitive in -οιο, and περίφρων Πηνελόπεια 'circumspect Penelope'. ἀνδρῶν … ἑκάστου is 'of each of the men', a partitive genitive, and ἐν μεγάροισιν 'in the halls' goes with ἀνδρῶν. μῦθον ἄκουεν is 'was hearing the talk'.

sentences.t:
δεῖπνον μὲν γάρ τοί γε γελοίωντες τετύκοντο
ἡδὺ τε καὶ μενοεικές, ἐπεὶ μάλα πόλλ’ ἱέρευσαν·
sentences.l:
For a meal, those men, laughing, were preparing
sweet and satisfying, since very many they had slaughtered;
sentences.i: For they, laughing, were preparing a meal, sweet and satisfying, since they had slaughtered a great many;
sentences.n: δεῖπνον μέν is answered by δόρπου δέ in 392: a 'meal' is being prepared, but the 'supper' will be something else. τοί γε is 'those men'. γελοίωντες is a variant spelling of the participle that line 374 spells γελόωντες. τετύκοντο is a reduplicated aorist middle of τεύχω 'make ready, prepare' (the English 'were preparing' gives it the progressive sense the context asks for). ἡδύ and μενοεικές, 'sweet' and 'satisfying', are neuter adjectives agreeing with δεῖπνον. ἱέρευσαν is the aorist of ἱερεύω 'slaughter', and πόλλ’ 'many things' means many animals. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
δόρπου δ’ οὐκ ἄν πως ἀχαρίστερον ἄλλο γένοιτο,
οἷον δὴ τάχ’ ἔμελλε θεὰ καὶ καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ
θησέμεναι·
sentences.i: But no other supper could ever be more graceless than the one that a goddess and a strong man were soon to set before them;
sentences.n: δόρπου is a genitive standing first, 'as for a supper' (it can also go with the comparative ἀχαρίστερον, 'than a supper'); δόρπον is the evening meal, set against δεῖπνον in 390. ἀχαρίστερον is the comparative of ἀχάριστος 'graceless', from ἀ- and χάρις. οὐκ ἄν πως … γένοιτο is 'could in no way come to be'. οἷον … θησέμεναι is 'such as … were going to set', with ἔμελλε and the future infinitive of τίθημι. The singular ἔμελλε has two subjects, θεά (Athena, named at 345) and καρτερὸς ἀνήρ (Odysseus, the 'father' of 385). The ano teleia ends the unit in the middle of 394.

sentences.t: πρότεροι γὰρ ἀεικέα μηχανόωντο.
sentences.l: for earlier they were devising unseemly things.
sentences.i: for they were the first to devise unseemly deeds.
sentences.n: The narrator gives his verdict. πρότεροι is 'earlier, first', in the predicate, and μηχανόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of μηχανάομαι 'devise'. ἀεικέα, 'unseemly', picks up ἀείκεια, ἀεικέα and ἀεικελίως from Telemachus’ speech at 308, 317 and 319: the vocabulary of what is unseemly returns to be turned against the suitors.
